name: OSI Model
summary: The OSI model is a 7-layer reference model that explains how data moves from an application on one computer to an application on another computer.

sections.title: The 7 layers (Layer 7 to Layer 1)
points: Layer 7 - Application: gives network services to the user. Examples: HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS, Telnet.
Layer 6 - Presentation: translates data format, does compression and encryption. Examples: JPEG, MPEG, SSL/TLS.
Layer 5 - Session: starts, manages and ends sessions between applications.
Layer 4 - Transport: end-to-end delivery, segmentation, flow control and error recovery. Protocols: TCP, UDP.
Layer 3 - Network: logical addressing and routing between networks. Protocols: IP, ICMP. Device: router.
Layer 2 - Data Link: physical (MAC) addressing, framing and error detection. Devices: switch, bridge, NIC.
Layer 1 - Physical: sends raw bits as electrical, light or radio signals. Devices: hub, cable, repeater.

sections.title: PDUs and devices
points: PDU names: Layer 7-5 = data, Layer 4 = segment, Layer 3 = packet, Layer 2 = frame, Layer 1 = bits.
Encapsulation adds a header at each layer while sending; de-encapsulation removes it while receiving.
Hub works at Layer 1, switch and bridge at Layer 2, router at Layer 3.
TCP/IP model maps as: Application = OSI 5-7, Transport = 4, Internet = 3, Network Access = 1-2.

sections.title: Easy memory trick
points: Top to bottom: All People Seem To Need Data Processing.
Bottom to top: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away.
If a question says "end-to-end delivery", the answer is the Transport layer.

name: TCP/IP
summary: TCP/IP is the practical protocol suite used on the Internet. TCP is reliable and connection-oriented, UDP is fast and connectionless.

sections.title: TCP basics
points: TCP is connection-oriented and reliable: it uses the 3-way handshake SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK before data is sent.
TCP numbers every byte (sequence number) and uses acknowledgements and retransmission to recover lost data.
Windowing controls how much data can be sent before waiting for an ACK (flow control).
TCP header flags: SYN (start), ACK (acknowledge), FIN (close), RST (reset), PSH (push), URG (urgent).
TCP is used for web, e-mail, file transfer and SSH where every byte must arrive.

sections.title: UDP basics
points: UDP is connectionless: no handshake, no acknowledgement and no retransmission.
UDP has less overhead and lower delay, so it is used for DNS, DHCP, TFTP, VoIP and video streaming.
A stateless protocol means the server responds and then forgets the request (example: HTTP).

sections.title: Port numbers to remember
points: FTP 20/21, SSH 22, Telnet 23, SMTP 25, DNS 53, DHCP 67/68, TFTP 69, HTTP 80.
POP3 110, NTP 123, IMAP 143, SNMP 161/162, HTTPS 443, TACACS+ 49, RADIUS 1812/1813.

name: IPv4 and IPv6
summary: IPv4 is a 32-bit address used today. IPv6 is a 128-bit address made to solve IPv4 address shortage.

sections.title: IPv4 address classes
points: Class A: 1-126 (first bit 0), Class B: 128-191 (first bits 10), Class C: 192-223 (first bits 110).
Class D: 224-239 is for multicast. Class E: 240-255 is experimental.
Loopback address is 127.0.0.1 (127.0.0.0/8) - it tests the local TCP/IP stack.
APIPA 169.254.0.0/16 is used when a DHCP client cannot get an address.

sections.title: IPv6 basics
points: IPv6 is 128 bits, written as 8 groups of 4 hex digits, e.g. 2001:0db8::1.
The :: sign replaces one block of all-zero groups only once in an address.
IPv6 has no broadcast. It uses unicast, multicast and anycast.
Link-local address starts with fe80::/10 and is used on the local segment.
EUI-64 builds the last 64 bits of an IPv6 address from the 48-bit MAC address.
IPv6 header is simpler: no checksum and routers do not fragment packets.

name: Subnetting
summary: Subnetting divides one network into smaller networks using a subnet mask, so broadcast domains stay small and addresses are used better.

sections.title: Formula and quick numbers
points: Number of hosts in a subnet = 2 raised to host bits, minus 2 (network and broadcast addresses).
Block size in an octet = 256 minus the mask value in that octet.
Network address = all host bits 0. Broadcast address = all host bits 1.
The first usable address is network + 1, the last usable is broadcast - 1.

sections.title: CIDR and VLSM
points: CIDR (classless) shows the mask as /n, e.g. 192.168.1.0/26 means 26 network bits.
VLSM gives different subnet masks to different subnets so no address is wasted.
CIDR summarization joins many small networks into one route entry.
Example: 172.17.175.122/25 has block size 128, so network = 172.17.175.0, broadcast = 172.17.175.127, usable = .1 to .126.

name: Routing
summary: Routing is the process of choosing the best path for a packet between different networks. Routers forward by the routing table.

sections.title: Routing basics
points: A router keeps a routing table; the longest matching prefix wins.
Default route 0.0.0.0/0 sends unknown destination traffic to the next hop.
Static routes are added manually and do not change automatically.
Dynamic protocols learn routes automatically when the topology changes.
Administrative distance shows trust: connected 0, static 1, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, RIP 120.

sections.title: Routing protocols
points: RIP is distance-vector, uses hop count, maximum 15 hops, updates every 30 seconds.
OSPF is link-state, uses cost (bandwidth), builds areas and elects DR/BDR.
EIGRP is an advanced hybrid protocol from Cisco, uses bandwidth and delay as its metric.
Metric is the value inside one protocol; administrative distance compares different protocols.

name: Switching
summary: A switch works at Layer 2 and forwards frames using MAC addresses. It learns addresses and builds a MAC table (CAM table).

sections.title: How a switch works
points: The switch learns the source MAC and port and stores it in the MAC table.
Unknown destination frames are flooded to all ports except the incoming port.
Known destination frames are forwarded only to the correct port.
Each switch port is its own collision domain; a VLAN is one broadcast domain.
Full duplex allows send and receive at the same time; half duplex uses CSMA/CD.

sections.title: Spanning Tree Protocol (STP)
points: STP stops Layer 2 loops by blocking extra links and keeping one active path.
Root bridge is the switch with the lowest bridge ID (priority + MAC).
Port states: blocking, listening, learning, forwarding, disabled.
STP timers: hello 2 seconds, forward delay 15 seconds, max age 20 seconds.
Port security limits which MAC addresses are allowed on a port.

name: VLAN
summary: A VLAN is a logical LAN made inside switches. It divides one switch into separate broadcast domains without new hardware.

sections.title: VLAN basics
points: VLAN 1 is the default VLAN. VLAN IDs for users are 1-1001 (1002-1005 are reserved).
Access port carries one VLAN for end devices; trunk port carries many VLANs between switches.
802.1Q adds a 4-byte tag with a 12-bit VLAN ID to the frame.
Native VLAN traffic goes over a trunk without a tag (always keep it a separate unused VLAN).
Inter-VLAN communication needs a router or a Layer 3 switch (router-on-a-stick uses subinterfaces).

sections.title: VTP
points: VTP shares the VLAN database between switches in the same domain.
VTP modes: server (can add/change VLANs), client (learns only), transparent (local only, forwards VTP messages).
A higher VTP revision number can overwrite the VLAN database, so change VLANs carefully.

name: NAT
summary: NAT translates private IP addresses into public IP addresses, saving IPv4 space and hiding internal hosts from the Internet.

sections.title: Types of NAT
points: Static NAT: one private IP maps to one public IP, used for servers.
Dynamic NAT: a private IP takes any free address from a public pool.
PAT (NAT overload): many private IPs share one public IP by using different port numbers.
NAT works on a router: interfaces are marked inside or outside.
Commands: ip nat inside, ip nat outside, ip nat inside source list 1 interface gi0/0 overload.

sections.title: Remember
points: NAT saves public IPv4 addresses and hides the internal network.
NAT can break end-to-end protocols such as IPsec VPN and some voice/video applications.
Private range plus NAT is why the Internet still works with IPv4 today.

name: WAN
summary: A WAN connects LANs that are far apart. It uses service provider links such as leased lines, MPLS and broadband.

sections.title: WAN links and encapsulation
points: Serial links use DTE (router side) and DCE (service provider side) devices; clock rate is set on the DCE.
HDLC is the default encapsulation on Cisco serial links but is proprietary to Cisco.
PPP is an open standard used between different vendors and supports authentication.
PPP uses LCP to set up the link and NCP for each network protocol.
Frame Relay uses PVC (permanent virtual circuits) and DLCI numbers to identify circuits.

sections.title: WAN services
points: Leased line gives a dedicated fixed bandwidth between two sites.
MPLS is a provider network that carries many customer networks with labels.
Broadband (DSL/cable) is cheaper but shared and not symmetric.
Always ask for CIR (committed information rate) in Frame Relay to know the guaranteed speed.

name: Wireless Networks
summary: Wireless LAN (Wi-Fi) uses radio waves instead of cables. 802.11 is the standard family and WPA2/WPA3 protect the traffic.

sections.title: 802.11 standards
points: 802.11b: 11 Mbps on 2.4 GHz. 802.11g: 54 Mbps on 2.4 GHz.
802.11a: 54 Mbps on 5 GHz. 802.11n: up to 600 Mbps with MIMO on 2.4/5 GHz.
802.11ac: above 1 Gbps on 5 GHz. 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) improves efficiency in crowded areas.
In 2.4 GHz the non-overlapping channels are 1, 6 and 11.
Wireless uses CSMA/CA (collision avoidance), not CSMA/CD.

sections.title: Wireless security
points: WEP is broken and must not be used.
WPA used TKIP and is now weak; WPA2 uses AES/CCMP and is still common.
WPA3 uses SAE and protects weak passwords better.
Enterprise mode (802.1X with EAP) authenticates each user through a RADIUS server.
SSID is the wireless network name; hiding it is not real security.

name: Network Security
summary: Network security protects confidentiality, integrity and availability (CIA) using passwords, ACLs, AAA and secure protocols.

sections.title: Device security
points: enable secret is stored encrypted (MD5); enable password is stored in clear text, so use enable secret.
service password-encryption hides clear-text passwords in the configuration.
Telnet sends data in clear text; SSH encrypts the session, so use SSH.
Set an exec-timeout so idle sessions close automatically.
AAA means Authentication (who you are), Authorization (what you can do), Accounting (what you did).

sections.title: ACLs and AAA servers
points: Standard ACL (1-99) filters only the source IP address.
Extended ACL (100-199) filters source, destination, protocol and port.
Every ACL ends with an implicit deny, so add an explicit permit when needed.
TACACS+ uses TCP 49 and encrypts the whole packet; RADIUS uses UDP 1812/1813 and hides only the password.
Port security, DHCP snooping and dynamic ARP inspection block Layer 2 attacks.

name: Networking Protocols
summary: These are the helper protocols that make a network work: ARP finds MAC addresses, ICMP reports errors, DNS resolves names and DHCP gives IP addresses.

sections.title: Address and control protocols
points: ARP finds the MAC address for a known IP address using a broadcast request and unicast reply.
ARP cache stores the mapping for a short time; arp -a shows it.
ICMP reports errors and is used by ping (echo request/reply) and traceroute (TTL expiry).
ICMP does not use TCP or UDP ports.
RARP is the old way to get an IP from a MAC; DHCP replaced it.

sections.title: Service protocols
points: DNS resolves names to IP addresses (port 53).
DHCP gives IP address, mask, gateway and DNS servers (ports 67/68).
SNMP monitors devices (161) and sends traps (162).
FTP uses TCP 20/21; TFTP uses UDP 69 and has no login.
SMTP sends mail (25), POP3 (110) and IMAP (143) receive mail.

name: DNS and DHCP
summary: DNS changes names into IP addresses. DHCP gives IP addresses and other settings to hosts automatically.

sections.title: DNS
points: DNS is a hierarchy: root, then TLD (.com, .in), then the domain and its authoritative server.
Recursive query: the server does all the work for the client. Iterative query: the server returns the next server to ask.
Common records: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), NS (name server), PTR (reverse lookup).
Forward lookup: name to IP. Reverse lookup: IP to name, in the in-addr.arpa zone.
DNS uses UDP 53 for normal queries and TCP 53 for large answers and zone transfers.
A DNS cache shortens lookup time. The SOA and NS records describe a zone.

sections.title: DHCP
points: DHCP uses DORA: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.
Server port is 67, client port is 68.
A scope is a range of addresses; a reservation always gives the same address to one MAC.
Lease time controls how long a client keeps the address.
A DHCP relay agent forwards DHCP messages between subnets.
